title: ARIA attributes must follow the element's rules
summary: An ARIA attribute is used in a way its element does not allow, such as aria-checked on a native checkbox. Remove it and rely on the native state.
problem: An ARIA attribute is allowed on the role but only under certain conditions, and this element breaks them. For example, a native <input type="checkbox"> already has its own checked state, so adding aria-checked can disagree with it and is not permitted.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users can be told the control is checked while the box is empty, or the reverse. They act on the announcement, so they submit the wrong choices.
steps: Find the element and attribute in the scan result.
Check whether the element is a native control. A native checkbox, radio button or table cell already exposes its own state and position, so remove the duplicate ARIA attribute.
If you need aria-checked, use it only on a custom element with role="checkbox" and no native input type.
Keep the visible state and the exposed state coming from one source, the native checked property where possible.
before:
<input type="checkbox" id="remember" aria-checked="true">
<label for="remember">Remember my details</label>
after:
<input type="checkbox" id="remember" checked>
<label for="remember">Remember my details</label>
whyItMatters: Two sources of truth for one state drift apart, and the user hears the wrong one. This is a WCAG 4.1.2 Level A requirement (Name, Role, Value), the level that accessibility regulations and procurement requirements commonly build on.
howToCheck: Re-run the scan. Toggle the control and confirm in your accessibility inspector that the exposed checked state follows the visible one.
